title: Bernie Richter and the Sammy Davis show
summary: Stories about cellist Bernie Richter, Henry Bussey's remark and Bernie as contractor for a Sammy Davis Jr. show.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, Bernie, Bernie, no, the story of that he drove a cab was that he was so disgusted with the kickbacks that these theater orchestras were making that he just got out of the business. Yeah, yeah. And he says, I'll go drive a cab to make a livelihood. And that's what he did for quite a while. And then he came down here and had an audition with the Hillsburg one. Hillsburg.
And he was with the symphony. In fact, he's a damn good cello player. He was until he got sick. He ain't kidding.
I play too well right now.
But he still plays more. But he'll run the damn orchestra.

He plays more than anybody that they got in the orchestra. But with all due respect to him, he's done shows. He's done, he's done, I don't know how many different shows in New York. And he knows what he's, he's not kidding you. He's not a bullshooter. Did Nappy leave the band
at the same time that Eddie did then? Nappy left us when we left the Edgewater. No, Eddie came with us. We put Angelo, we had Angelo Palmasana after that. Bernie's been very sick lately. Huh?

Who has? Oh, Bernie. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Yeah, Bernie plays well. But Bernie's in, the story that, what's the hot lips there? What's the matter? You remember the trumpet player? Dropped down a lot of sweet, uh.

Yeah, Henry Bussey. Yeah, I see him. He told me, he says, you know something? He says, in the orchestra, he says, from now on, he says, I want a, he says, I want a, I want a Jewish guy in my orchestra for luck. And he says, I want a dago in there to pimp on the Jew when he gets to, and he says, I'll be all right.

Henry Bussey told me. You want to hear a cute story about Bernie. Let me, let me get on with the owls here. We want to take one second. This is about when he was a conductor, contractor for the, uh, Sammy Davis Jr. show in New Orleans at the, the performing arts. And he wanted, oh, should have cut the book. And I mean, they, they got a book that, believe me, it takes a musician to cut it. And he got the best musicians in town to play the show. And they did a hell of a job. So coming down here, Sammy Davis brought five men with him. Three whites and two blacks. One was his leader who just died recently. And at the end of the performance, Bernie went in to thank him for engaging him as a contractor for the show. So Sammy Davis told him, he says, he says, I'm sorry that you didn't use more colored men in the orchestra than you did. Because you only used one. Well, he says, that's true. He says, but he says, you've got a book there that requires to be read and you've got to be professional business, professional musicians. He says, most of the colored people down here can't even read the titles of the tunes. Can't read the words on what the name of the tune is. He says, and I'm sorry, he says, in fact, you brought three blacks down here. Three whites and two blacks. You didn't judge a good relationship there. He says, and in fact, as a matter of fact, he says, we're both in a hell of a fix with the anti-defamation of the League and the B'nai B'rith. He says, why? He says, we're the only two Jews in the whole outfit.

Well, Bernie's got a tongue on him. But as a conductor, he could have never conducted anything. He can play. He can play. Put the music down in front of him and he'll play and he'll follow him. But I told him, Bernie, how the hell can you play the instruments so well and you know, shitting him about kicking off a tempo. I says, Christ's sake, and Lester starts slow and gets faster and faster or he starts fast and slows down.
